papers.summary: This retrospective study examined clinical placement records for 331 nursing graduates across four cohorts at a public university in Barcelona, Spain. It found that specialised care settings made up 75%-76% of placement weeks, while primary and transitional care made up much smaller shares, with transitional care underused despite open spots. This points to an imbalance in training exposure that may affect how programs coordinate placements with healthcare providers.

papers.title: Simulation‐Based Education to Support Nurses' Critical Thinking in Delirium Recognition: A Scoping Review.
papers.abstract: Aim: To map how simulation‐based education supports the development of critical thinking skills required for nurses to recognize delirium in clinical practice. Design: A scoping review guided by the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and the framework developed by Arksey and O'Malley, refined by Levac and colleagues. Methods: Two reviewers independently screened and extracted data to identify studies evaluating simulation‐based education designed to strengthen nurses' delirium recognition and associated critical thinking processes. A narrative approach was used to chart and synthesize findings across varied simulation modalities and clinical contexts. Data Sources: The search was conducted on 4 September 2025, using MEDLINE, CINAHL and PsycINFO. No timeframe was applied to the search. Results: Fourteen studies met inclusion criteria. Simulation‐based education consistently enhanced skills aligned with critical thinking, including observational accuracy, recognition of fluctuating cognitive cues, clinical reasoning, reflective awareness, empathy and communication within interprofessional teams. Structured debriefing played a central role in helping nurses analyse decision‐making processes and integrate experiential learning into clinical judgement. Several studies reported changes in practice, including more consistent use of delirium identification tools and improved clarity of clinical documentation. Conclusion: Simulation‐based education strengthens interconnected domains of critical thinking that underpin nurses' capacity to recognize delirium early and respond effectively to its fluctuating presentation. These findings highlight the educational value of immersive, theory‐informed simulation for developing the clinical judgement required in cognitively complex patient situations. Implications for the Profession and/or Patient Care: Integrating structured simulation into nursing education and professional development may enhance timely delirium recognition, foster more effective interprofessional communication and support safer, higher‐quality care for hospitalized adults. Impact: Simulation‐based education offers a practical and scalable strategy for improving delirium recognition across care settings. By supporting nurses in noticing subtle cognitive changes, interpreting clinical patterns and communicating concerns with clarity and confidence, simulation contributes to stronger workforce preparedness and patient safety. Reporting Method: This review adhered to PRISMA‐ScR reporting guidance. Patient or Public Contribution: This study did not include patient or public involvement in its design, conduct or reporting. What Does This Paper Contribute to the Wider Global Clinical Community?: Clarifies how simulation strengthens the cognitive, reflective and communicative skills nurses require to recognize delirium promptly and accurately.Demonstrates that structured simulation and debriefing offer an efficient, scalable method to enhance clinical judgement and interprofessional communication across care settings.Consolidates global evidence to guide education, workforce development and future research aimed at improving delirium recognition and patient safety.
papers.authors:
EL Hussein, Mohamed Toufic
                Sheehan, Dawson S.
                Hirst, Sandra
                Faculty of Health, Community and Education, School of Nursing and Midwifery, Mount Royal University, Calgary, Canada
papers.journal: Journal of Advanced Nursing (John Wiley & Sons, Inc.)
papers.summary: This scoping review looked at 14 studies on simulation-based education and how it helps nurses think critically to recognize delirium in patients. The review found that simulation improved skills like spotting subtle cognitive changes, clinical reasoning, and teamwork, with structured debriefing helping nurses reflect on their decisions. This suggests simulation training could help nurses catch delirium earlier and communicate more clearly across care teams.

papers.title: Improving Haemorrhage Prediction in General Ward Patients by Incorporating Patterns of Change Derived From Routine Ward Measurements.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Aim  Design  Methods  Results  Conclusion  Implications for the Profession and/or Patient Care  Impact  Reporting Method  To evaluate whether patterns of change derived from routine ward measurements provide additional predictive value beyond the most recent clinical measurements for haemorrhage prediction in general ward patients.A retrospective cohort study.Among 16,197 adult patients admitted to general wards in three university‐affiliated hospitals in South Korea, 1152 (7.1%) experienced haemorrhage, whereas 15,045 (92.9%) did not. Three machine‐learning algorithms evaluated three feature sets based on the most recent clinical measurements, patterns of change or both. Models were trained and internally validated using stratified five‐fold cross‐validation. Predictive performance was compared across feature sets using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, sensitivity, specificity and F1‐score. Shapley Additive Explanations were used to interpret the best‐performing model.Models using both recent measurements and patterns of change showed small but statistically supported improvements in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve compared with models using recent measurements alone. Shapley Additive Explanations identified neutrophil count, platelet count, white blood cell count, urine output and vital signs as key predictors.Patterns of change derived from routine ward measurements provided complementary predictive information for haemorrhage prediction in general ward patients beyond the most recent clinical measurements. Routinely collected ward data may therefore contain additional predictive information not captured by the most recent values alone.Machine‐learning models combining recent clinical measurements with patterns of change may support risk stratification in general ward patients; prospective evaluation is needed to determine their clinical utility.The study examined whether patterns of change improve haemorrhage prediction. These findings suggest that routinely collected ward data may provide additional predictive information beyond the most recent clinical measurements. The potential value of this information for nursing surveillance and timely intervention warrants prospective evaluation.Transparent reporting of a multivariable prediction model for individual prognosis or diagnosis–artificial intelligence (TRIPOD + AI).

papers.journal: Journal of Clinical Nursing (John Wiley & Sons, Inc.)
papers.summary: Researchers studied over 16,000 general ward patients at three South Korean hospitals to see if tracking changes in routine measurements over time could improve haemorrhage prediction, beyond using only the most recent values. Machine-learning models combining both approaches showed small but statistically supported improvements, with neutrophil count, platelet count, white blood cell count, urine output, and vital signs as key predictors. This suggests routine ward data may hold extra value for nursing surveillance, though prospective testing is needed before clinical use.
